title: Made To Be Looked At
logline: A valley of paddy fields in the middle of a hill capital was turned into an ornamental lake two centuries ago, by labour the people owed to the crown by the size of their land, and the whole of it can be walked round in an hour, which is what several thousand people do every morning, because it is beautiful.
human_question: If what decides the kind of act something was is the aim it was done for, what am I supposed to do with a thing that is genuinely beautiful and genuinely cost what it cost?

place.what_kind_of_place: A made lake filling the floor of a small valley in the centre of a hill city, ringed on every side by steep wooded slopes and by the city itself. It is not a natural body of water and does not pretend to be: a single long bund of made ground closes the low end of the valley and carries a public road along its top, a low stone parapet runs the entire way round with a repeating wave or cloud form cut into it and small triangular openings at intervals, two streams come in off the hills at the upper end, and a single small island near the middle carries one small building. The whole perimeter is a continuous public footway of roughly three kilometres which returns a walker to the exact point they started from. A large royal-period temple complex stands on the northern shore; this film keeps it at the far side of the water and never goes in.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Four things carry it with the sound off, and all four are at eye level. Mist, which forms on the water before sunrise and sits inside the ring of hills so that the far shore is a rumour and the near parapet is the only hard edge in the frame. The wall itself, which is the most photogenic piece of stonework in the country and repeats the same carved swell for six hundred metres, so a lens laid along it turns the whole circuit into one long rhythm. The island, which is in the middle distance from almost every point on the walk, is never any nearer, and cannot be reached. And the closing of the circuit: because the path is a ring, the film's last frame is its first frame, in different light, with the mist gone.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Everything that changes is weather, water and a city waking, and none of it is arranged. Mist forms, thickens and burns off inside about forty minutes. The water surface goes from black to grey to a hard bright sheet. Cormorants and egrets work the shallows and roost in the trees along the bank. Water level moves with the monsoon and the two feeder streams. And the human traffic changes completely across the morning: almost nobody at first light, then walkers, then school traffic and buses on the bund road, then, by mid-morning, a continuous slow line of people along the parapet, standing at it and looking at the water.
place.when_it_looks_best: First light, and specifically the pre-sunrise half hour, which is when the mist exists and when the parapet can be filmed without a crowd on it. Overcast and post-rain light suit the stone better than sun, which flattens the carving. The second monsoon months give the best mist and the highest water; the driest months give the worst of both. The mid-morning crowd beat needs full light and is filmed long, from across the water.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: One lap of a lake on foot, at ground level, in one morning. Mist on black water inside a bowl of hills; a carved stone wall running away from the camera; an island that never gets closer; a city filling up behind the parapet; and then the same length of wall the film opened on, with the mist gone and people leaning on it. It resolves entirely on its own terms, because a ring closes: the piece ends where it began and the only thing that has changed is the light and how many people are looking at the water. No drone, no reveal, no summit.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the sources' two separate pages about a made thing. One page takes a purposeful act apart into the parts that assemble it — arriving at something, going over it, settling on it, pushing it through, the gladness in it, the plain wish to do it — and insists that not one of those parts is good or bad in itself. The other page sorts acts by aim rather than by act, and its list of everyday occasions for a grasping mind includes, in so many words, looking at a beautiful thing for the pleasure of looking. The film puts those two pages on a lake that was made to be beautiful and was built by compelled labour, states what the record actually carries and what it does not, and then stops. The voice never delivers a verdict on anybody, because neither page is a verdict.

sequence.on_screen: Before sunrise, at the parapet. Mist lying on black water; the far shore not visible; the carved top of the wall in the near foreground going out of frame. No people yet.
sequence.voice: This valley floor was paddy fields. Sri Wickrama Rajasinha, the last king to hold this country, had them flooded into a lake, and every account of why says the same thing: it was to make the palace and the temples beside it more beautiful. It worked. Two hundred years later this is the most looked-at water on the island.

sequence.on_screen: The wall. A long lens laid down its length so the repeated carved swell stacks into one rhythm, then close: the small triangular openings cut through it at intervals, empty.
sequence.voice: The compendium this series reads keeps a long and perfectly frank list of the ordinary occasions on which a grasping mind comes up. Drink, gambling, music, song, scent, fine clothes, good food, games, getting money and guarding it, making and using pleasing things, houses, carriages, clothes. And this, word for word: looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking. Not making them. Looking at them.

sequence.on_screen: The bund: one straight line of made ground closing the low end of the valley, water on one side and the town dropping away on the other, a road along its top with early traffic on it.
sequence.voice: This line is the whole lake. It is a dam, and the people who built it owed the work. John Davy, who was in the country within a year or two of the king's removal, set the obligation down exactly: people were liable to be called to labour at public works — making roads, levelling hills, excavating tanks — and according to the size of their land-holdings they might be employed at it fifteen to thirty days a year. The books are careful about what they call effort. It is mental rather than muscular, and it has no colour of its own: in a mind already leaning one way it runs like a boat on water flowing downhill, and doing something good with it is described as carrying a load up a hill. Effort was never the part that decided anything.

sequence.on_screen: The island, from three separate points on the walk: the same small building at the same middle distance each time, never nearer. A boat is not taken.
sequence.voice: Somebody settled this. Pilimatalawe, the first minister, told the king to his face that the works were vexatious to the people and oppressive; Davy wrote that down. It is also widely said that about a hundred headmen were impaled on this bund for refusing the work. That account appears only in modern writing, the early record does not carry it, and this film states it once and does not picture it. What the books say about settling is this: the factor that comes down on a thing does it without sorting true from false or good from bad, and they add, with no softening at all, that it is very often perfectly firm and wrong.

sequence.on_screen: The far side of the water at full light. A temple roofline at distance across the lake, held for a moment, not approached. Then back to the wall and the water below it.
sequence.voice: The same page that lists the occasions also exempts. Where faith, loving-kindness, compassion or plain practical sense goes in front of an act, it says flatly that no unwholesome mind arises for it. Food cooked against hunger, not for the taste. Cloth worn against cold and insects. Even a costly, beautiful garment, when it is worn to escape being looked down on. Beauty itself is not on that list. In the expectation of being beautiful is on the other side of the line. And the cost of a thing is not weighed on that page at all: the harm is dealt with elsewhere, where seven courses of harm are named and taking what is not given is one of them. Two pages. The books do not add them up, and neither does this film.

sequence.on_screen: The upper end: the two streams coming in off the hills, shallow and clear, and the water they arrive into. Cormorants working the margin; egrets in the bank trees.
sequence.voice: There is one more part, and it is the part the whole group turns on. The books call it the wish to do. They say it looks a little like grasping and is not: it is wanting with none of the sticking in it. In a grasping mind it goes along with the grasping. In a mind set against grasping it works against it. And trained, they say, it becomes a base of success, and carries a person as far as a person can go.

sequence.on_screen: Mid-morning, long lens from across the water: a continuous slow line of people along the parapet, standing at it, looking at the lake. Nobody held, nobody's face the subject, the crowd read as a rhythm along the wall.
sequence.voice: Several thousand times a morning, the thing does the job it was made for. The books would sort every one of those minds by three things — whether the feeling in it is glad or flat, whether a wrong view is joined to it, and whether it came up by itself or had to be urged — and they list eight of them. Not one of the three can be photographed. What is on this side of the wall is a beautiful thing being looked at. Which mind is doing the looking is not in the frame, and was never going to be.

sequence.on_screen: The same stretch of parapet the film opened on. Mist gone, water bright, people leaning on the wall. The lap is closed; the frame matches the first shot.
sequence.voice: The deciding was firm. The effort had no colour of its own. The wish to do it was not the same thing as the wanting that sticks. The lake is here, and it is beautiful, and it was owed by somebody. Nothing on either page turns any of that into a verdict on the man who settled it. His kingdom ended three years after the wall was finished, and the books do not offer that as a consequence of anything. They are an account of what a mind was made of in a moment. They are not a ledger of what a life deserved.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the two digests describe a made thing from two directions and neither is a moral scoreboard. C021 is the anatomy: six factors that turn up in some minds and not others, across wholesome and unwholesome alike, each taking the colour of whatever mind it joins [C021-P:L25], which is why a film can show an enormous work without praising or condemning it. Its parts are all here at eye level. The settling factor comes down on an object without sorting true from false or good from bad, and the Pradeepika says outright that it is very often firm and wrong [C021-P:L45], with the Margaya adding that it takes the object one way, rightly or wrongly, and is hard to discern at all [C021-M:L15]. Effort is mental rather than bodily [C021-M:L19] and flows the way the ground slopes — like a boat on water running downhill in a mind bent to harm, against the load carried up a hill that doing good requires [C021-P:L53]. Arriving on an object and going over it are a bell's stroke and the ring that follows, which the Margaya warns is not a sequence [C021-M:L11] and the Pradeepika pictures as one hand holding a vessel firmly while the other slowly polishes it [C021-P:L41] [C021-P:L33]. And the load-bearing item: the wish to do is not greed, it lacks greed's stickiness [C021-P:L69], it goes with greed in a greed-rooted mind and against it in a mind set the other way [C021-M:L27], and developed it becomes a base of success leading as far as a person can go [C021-P:L75]. C005 supplies the classification, and it is the reason this location was chosen rather than any other reservoir. Its long list of everyday occasions includes making and using pleasing things and, in so many words, looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking [C005-M:L5], and it says most of an ordinary day runs on this [C005-M:L7]. Then it exempts, on aim: where faith, loving-kindness, compassion or practical discernment of usefulness goes in front, no unwholesome mind arises [C005-M:L9], and it exempts again for food against hunger [C005-M:L13] and cloth against cold and insects [C005-M:L17] and even a costly beautiful garment worn to escape contempt [C005-M:L19]. A lake made expressly to be beautiful is the exact case where those two pages meet, and the meeting is the film.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the sources classify the aim and not the scale, and that this is not the same as forgiving the scale. The exemptions were tested against this film's own subject and they do not cover it: the aim named in the exempting column is faith, kindness, compassion or use [C005-M:L9], and beauty as an aim is named on the other side — in the expectation of being beautiful, of taking others' minds, of appearing superior [C005-M:L15] — while the one ruling that lets a beautiful and costly thing through does so for escaping contempt and not for the beauty [C005-M:L19], and the digest itself flags that ruling as needing an expert check. So making a thing beautiful falls outside the exemptions and inside the list. But the list is not a condemnation: the digest's own limit says music, dance and games appear there because of the enjoying mind and not because the arts are condemned, and a film must not imply otherwise. What the pairing produces is therefore the opposite of an indictment. The cost of this lake is not weighed on the ornament page at all; it belongs to the separate page where seven courses of harm are named, taking what is not given among them [C005-M:L3]. C021 finishes the job by removing the last three places a verdict could hide: effort is not a virtue and carries nothing on its own [C021-P:L53], certainty is not evidence and the settling that made this was firm in exactly the way the sources say is usually wrong [C021-P:L45], and the drive behind it was not itself the grasping [C021-P:L69] [C021-M:L27]. The film can therefore state the purpose, state the labour, state the disputed atrocity once with its evidential standing attached, and hand the viewer two pages that were never designed to be added together.

concept_links.why: The digest supplies the film's spine and, crucially, its refusals. The occasional factors are ethically variable and take the colour of the mind they join [C021-P:L25], so a work of this size can be filmed without the footage becoming an accusation. The settling factor is beat 4: it fastens on an object without distinguishing true from false or good from bad and is frequently firm and wrong [C021-P:L45], and the Margaya notes it is hard to make out at all [C021-M:L15] — which is what a documented objection by a first minister and an undocumented atrocity story look like side by side. Effort is beat 3: mental rather than muscular [C021-M:L19], sliding easily to harm like a boat on water running downhill and needing deliberate application to go the other way, as a load carried uphill [C021-P:L53]. The bell's stroke and its after-ring, held simultaneous and not sequential [C021-M:L11] [C021-P:L41], and the hand that grips while the other polishes [C021-P:L41], are the film's method rather than its narration — one lap, arriving and going over. Beat 6 is the digest's most load-bearing claim: the wish to do lacks greed's sticking [C021-P:L69], accords with greed in a greed-rooted mind and opposes it in a mind set against it [C021-M:L27], and developed becomes a base of success reaching to the end [C021-P:L75]. Four of the digest's limits are written into the beats rather than kept as cautions. No 'follow your passion': drive inside a greed-rooted mind guarantees nothing, which is beat 3's point about the slope. No 'desire is the enemy': on the wish to do the sources say the opposite, which is beat 6. No 'hard work is virtuous': effort is neutral in the source and this lake is the largest possible demonstration of it, which is why beat 3 refuses to admire the labour and beat 8 repeats the refusal. And no 'trust your gut': the deciding that made this was firm, and the digest says firm is not right. The digest's traditional physiology — rapture moving the body through the air element, and the vitakka sound audible to the divine ear — is not narrated, and the five kinds of rapture [C021-P:L61] [C021-P:L63] are deliberately left out of the film because putting a named bodily gladness onto people on a public parapet would make them exhibits.

C005 is why this location and not another, and the link was rewritten after reading the exemptions against the film's own case rather than inheriting a reading. The Margaya's list of occasions is frank and enormous, and two of its items are this lake exactly: preparing and using pleasing things, and looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking [C005-M:L5]; it adds that for people living apart from the teaching most minds from waking to sleep are of this kind [C005-M:L7]. The exemptions are real and are stated in the film: faith, loving-kindness, compassion or practical discernment of usefulness in front of an act, and no unwholesome mind arises [C005-M:L9]; food for hunger and for keeping life going [C005-M:L13]; cloth against cold, heat and insects [C005-M:L17]; a beautiful and even valuable garment worn to escape the contempt of onlookers [C005-M:L19]. Read straight, they do not reach making something beautiful. Beauty as the aim is named on the greed side, in the expectation of being beautiful, of taking others' minds, of appearing as a superior person [C005-M:L15], as is food prepared for the relish or for the body's comeliness [C005-M:L11] and the beautiful animal caught and kept in order to be looked at [C005-M:L23]. The film says so and then stops, because the digest's limits forbid every step further. 'Art and sport are sinful' is named and refused, so a lake made to be beautiful is not narrated as a sin and no shot is composed to make it look like one. 'Minimalism' and 'self-denial is virtue' are refused, since the source allows valuable clothes and wealth wisely earned, so the film never implies the right course was to build nothing. 'Only intentions matter' is refused, which is the guard that matters most here: the source still names particular actions as courses of harm carried out through wanting, seven of the ten, taking what is not given among them [C005-M:L3], so the compulsion cannot be dissolved into a question about a dead man's motives. The Pradeepika's extract supplies only the eight greed-rooted minds and the three conditions that separate them — feeling, view and prompting [C005-P:L12] [C005-P:L27–L42] — which is beat 7's whole point: three conditions, none of them photographable. The digest's own uncertainty about the contempt ruling [C005-M:L19] is treated as binding: the film does not use it to argue that a king's display was exempt.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the sources are sorting aims, not sizes, and that this is a narrower instrument than it first looks. Where faith, kindness, compassion or plain usefulness goes in front of an act, the books say no unwholesome mind arises for it — and beauty is not one of those four, so a thing made to be beautiful sits in the list rather than in the exemptions, which is a classification and not a sentence. Meanwhile the cost of the thing is judged somewhere else entirely, on the page about courses of harm. A viewer who takes only one thing should take this: the effort in a great work is not the part that decided anything, the certainty behind it was probably firm and may have been wrong, and none of that is a verdict on anybody, because the books describe a moment in a mind and not the deserts of a life.
what_must_be_real: The walk in the order a walker actually meets it, at the lake's own hours, with the mist filmed on whatever morning it forms. Nothing is reconstructed: no re-enactment, no actors, no period dressing, no impalement imagery, no stake, no silhouette, no shot on the bund composed to suggest what is said to have happened there, and no sound design standing in for it. The atrocity claim is spoken once, in one place, with its evidential standing attached in the same breath, and it is never illustrated. The temple complex on the northern shore is not entered, no interior is filmed, no observance or worship is filmed anywhere, no offering is shown, and the most that appears is a roofline across the water at distance in a single held shot. People on the parapet are a city at its own business: filmed long, in motion, nobody held, nobody followed, no face the subject of a frame, nobody asked why they come, and nobody presented as looking at beautiful water for pleasure — the voice makes the classification and the framing never applies it to a person. No drone. The two dates, the two versions of the atrocity story and the disagreements about the lake's area, depth and the wall's proper name go on screen as disagreements if they go on screen at all, and are never resolved for tidiness. No verdict on the last king, no verdict on the chiefs, and no line, shot or cut that connects the making of this lake to the end of the kingdom.
position_hint: late in the group: the film that tests the group's own instrument, after the simpler films about wanting have established what the instrument is. It needs a viewer who already knows the sources sort by aim, because its whole argument is what happens when that sorting is applied to something magnificent and compelled at once. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: The indictment. The obvious film here is a doctrinal prosecution of a dead king, and both digests forbid it. C005's limits refuse 'art and sport are sinful' and refuse 'minimalism' and 'self-denial is virtue'; C021 says every factor takes the colour of the mind it joins and none is good or bad in itself. Any frame, cut or line that makes the lake look like a moral error breaks the record this film is built on.

Kamma as fate. The kingdom fell three years after the work was finished and the temptation to let one follow from the other is enormous. It is the floor's hardest line and beat 8 exists to refuse it out loud. No dissolve from the wall to the cession, no narration of decline, no 'and then'.

Dwelling on the atrocity. Stated once, flat, with its standing attached, and never pictured. The specific failure to guard against is a shot of the bund at dusk, or a held empty stretch of parapet with the claim over it, which would be a reconstruction by framing.

Overstating the claim in the other direction. The early record is silent on a hundred impaled here, but silence is not disproof, and the film must not narrate the story as invented or as slander. It says what the sources are and how late they are.

The temple. It stands on this water, it is one of the most venerated places in the Buddhist world, and a film about wanting has no business inside it. Nothing is filmed in it, no beat rests on it, no worship is filmed, and a distant roofline is the ceiling.

Nobody on the parapet is an exhibit. The camera cannot show which mental factor is present and the digests say so. The crowd is filmed as a rhythm along a wall, long and in motion; no identifiable person is framed as devout, acquisitive, idle or delighted, and no face carries the argument.

Leaning on the contempt exemption. The Margaya's ruling that a beautiful and costly garment worn to escape contempt is not unwholesome is the one exemption that could be stretched into a defence of royal display, and the digest itself records it as odd and wanting an expert check. The film states the exemption as written and never applies it to the king.
'Follow your passion' and 'hard work is virtuous', which are the two readings C021 names and refuses. A great work built at great cost invites both.

Certainty as evidence. The film repeats the sources' claim that the settling factor is firm and frequently wrong. Applied to a named historical decision it would slide into a verdict, so it is stated as doctrine and left there.

Drone. This water sits inside a World Heritage sacred city beside a principal temple, and a drone over it would be both a permissions problem and the wrong film. Drone is treated as prohibited and the high wide view, if the film needs one at all, comes from a public hillside viewpoint on a long lens.
Consent on a public footway in a busy city, in languages the crew may not share, at a place where many of the people walking are visiting the temple.

The group's other water. GRP-02's films must not converge; this one is deliberately the only one built on a closed circuit at ground level with no aerial payoff, and that has to survive production pressure.
drop_if: The mist does not form in any workable window, which removes the first-light half of the film and with it the reason the walk is at ground level.
The lake cannot be filmed without an arrangement that makes the temple a participant, which would put the film inside a place it has undertaken to stay out of.
The atrocity claim cannot be stated once without becoming the film's subject in the edit.
The only way to obtain the circuit is a drone, or the footway proves unfilmable at first light for safety or access reasons.

connections.note: The group's other film on a king's works and on C021's account of effort: eleven years of unfinished carving on a rock, and a finished ornament still in daily use two centuries on. Neither film admires the effort, and the pair shows why — the sources say effort carries nothing on its own.

The slate's other film built on C005's exemptions rather than its list: a room made to be beautiful, and a lake made to be beautiful. That film found the exemption; this one found its edge, and the two together show where the line actually falls.
An aim that cannot be located in the thing made, and a flavour that cannot be located in the leaf.

selection.reason: A landmark whose documented history asks C005's own question — an ornament, a stated purpose of beauty, and labour owed by tenure — and where C021's account of effort, settling and the wish to do can be filmed on a closed circuit at ground level without a single aerial shot, which also gives the group a treatment nothing else in it shares.

review.note: Rewritten from the ground up on 2026-09-26 under the GRP-02 reassignment, and the verdict is reset because the body is a different film. The old film went because it failed the standard directly: it was a village that makes drums and teaches dance, a working place carrying the concepts by analogy, with no chronicled or disputed story in it, and its payoff was an overhead shot of a rehearsal that may not be obtainable at all; it also put a camera on young trainees in a group about greed, which the floor makes very hard to hold. The new film is a made lake in the centre of a hill capital, and the historical binding is documentary rather than analogical. The site was a paddy flat; the last king of the country had it flooded; the modern heritage literature is unanimous that the purpose was to increase the beauty of the palace complex and the temples beside it; and the labour was rajakariya, the service people owed the crown, which John Davy — in the country within a year or two of the king's removal — describes precisely as a liability to labour at public works, making roads, levelling hills and excavating tanks, for fifteen to thirty days a year according to land-holding. That is C005's page on aim standing in the open: a thing made expressly to be looked at, and the exemptions read against it. The impalement claim at the centre of the row was tested hard and does not stand where the row placed it. No contemporary or colonial-era narrative source found carries it: Davy's account of the reign (1821) and Henry Marshall's (1846) both give impalement episodes with specific numbers — six petty chiefs hanged and impaled in 1812, forty-seven prisoners impaled in 1814 — and neither connects any of them to the lake. What Davy does record, within a few years of the events, is the objection itself: the first minister Pilimatalawe told the king that the public works, listed as several new roads, the lake, and new buildings, were vexatious to the people and oppressive. The hundred-impaled-on-the-bund story circulates only in modern popular writing, in two mutually incompatible versions (a hundred headmen who refused the labour, or a hundred advisers who counselled against the project), and the single citation offered anywhere traces to a 2005 Sri Lankan newspaper column citing a D'Oyly despatch to Governor Brownrigg 'vide Ceylon Literary Register, Vol. IV', which could not be verified and carries two internal problems: D'Oyly's stated office is anachronistic for 1814, and the date given, Vesak poya day 23 May 1814, was not a full-moon day. The film therefore stands on the labour and the purpose and states the claim once, flat, with its standing attached, with no reconstruction and no shot framed to evoke it. The title changed accordingly: the row proposed 'A Hundred Who Said No', which asserts as fact the one thing the research could not support, so the film is called 'Made To Be Looked At', after the stated purpose and after the one item in C005's list that survives every exemption. Both concept links were re-tested against their digests and rewritten. The guards: no verdict on the king and none on the kingdom's fall, with beat 8 written to refuse the causal reading out loud; the temple on the northern shore is never entered, no beat rests on it, no worship is filmed and a distant roofline is the ceiling; nobody on the parapet is framed as looking at beautiful water for pleasure, because the camera cannot show which mind is present; drone is treated as prohibited over a World Heritage sacred city, which is also what gives the group its only ground-level closed-circuit treatment. Five Wikimedia Commons images were confirmed through the query API.

suggested_location.name: Kandy Lake (Kiri Muhuda)

also_known_as.name: Kiri Muhuda
also_known_as.used_by: the name recorded for the pond that stood in the middle of the paddy flat, carried over to the lake built on it

also_known_as.name: Nuwara Wewa
also_known_as.used_by: ordinary Sinhala usage; the same name belongs to a much older and larger tank in another district, so it is ambiguous

also_known_as.name: Tigolwela
also_known_as.meaning: the name of the stretch of paddy fields that occupied the valley floor before the lake
also_known_as.used_by: the pre-1800 name of the site

suggested_location.region: Kandy District, Central Province, in the valley floor at the centre of the city, immediately south of the royal palace and temple precinct
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place that puts both concepts in the same frame at eye level. C005 sorts acts by the aim in front of them, and this is a large public object whose recorded aim was beauty and nothing else: the modern heritage literature is unanimous that the paddy flat was flooded to increase the beauty of the palace complex and the temples beside it, the parapet that rings it exists to be looked at and has lamp niches cut into it, and the island in the middle carries a pleasure building. Against that, the labour was rajakariya, owed to the crown by tenure, and the objection to the works as oppressive is recorded within a few years by a British writer who was there. So the exemption question — does making a thing beautiful fall inside the source's exemptions or outside them — is not a hypothetical the film has to construct; it is the actual history of the actual object. C021 then supplies the anatomy, and the place hands over each part physically: a single bund that is the whole decision made visible, an enormous quantity of effort surviving as a shape, and an island that is in the middle distance from every point on the walk and can never be reached. And the cinema is genuinely there without an aerial: mist inside a bowl of hills before sunrise, six hundred metres of carved stone that a long lens turns into one rhythm, and a ring path whose last frame is its first.

historical_thread.story:
The floor of the valley south of the royal palace at Kandy was a stretch of paddy fields called Tigolwela, and in the middle of it was a pond called Kiri-muhuda, the sea of milk. Sri Wickrama Rajasinha, who reigned from 1798 and was the last king of the country, had the paddy flat flooded into an ornamental lake, and the new water kept the old pond's name. Sri Lankan heritage sources name Deveda Moolacharya as the architect. The method was a dam thrown across the low end of the valley, beginning at the Paththirippuwa end of the palace precinct — where the steps down into the water from the Mahamaluwa esplanade are still visible — and running across to the Poya-maluwa; a roadway was carried along the top of it, which let the king cross to the Malwatte Vihare on the far side. Earth was taken from both ends, and an island was left standing in the middle, known as the Diyathilaka Mandapaya.

The date is not settled. 1807 is the figure repeated in almost all travel and reference writing, including the English Wikipedia article's opening sentence. Against it, the same article's own history section reports that according to D'Oyly the dam was built between 1810 and 1812, and the Sri Lankan heritage literature follows the 1810–1812 dating. John D'Oyly was the British government's chief translator from 1805 and its principal intelligence officer in the Kandyan interior in these years, so his is the closest thing to a contemporary administrative dating available; he became Resident and First Commissioner in the Kandyan Provinces only after the kingdom was ceded in 1815. Both figures are in circulation and neither has been checked here against a primary text.

The purpose is recorded consistently and the labour is recorded precisely. Every modern account of the lake states that it was built to increase the aesthetic beauty of the royal palace complex and the temples around it, and that rajakariya — the compulsory service owed to the crown — supplied the workforce. No contemporary statement of purpose in the king's own words, or in a chronicle, was located in this research; the ornamental reading rests on the modern literature and on the character of the works themselves, which are a parapet with lamp niches, an island pavilion and a lake with no irrigation command. What rajakariya actually was, however, is set down by a near-contemporary: John Davy, brother of Humphry Davy, was in the island from 1816 and published An Account of the Interior of Ceylon in 1821, and he describes the obligation as it stood before the British took over. People 'were liable to be called on to labour at certain public works, as in making roads, levelling hills, and excavating tanks; and, according to the extent of their land-tenures, they might be employed annually in such services, from fifteen to thirty days.' The system was abolished in 1832 on the recommendation of the Colebrooke–Cameron Commission.

The objection to the works is documented, and it is the film's centre. Davy, writing of the quarrel between the king and his first minister Pilimatalawe, records that 'the minister expressed his disapprobation of the public works which the king was then engaged in, on the ground that they were vexatious to the people and oppressive. The works in question were several new roads; the lake of Kandy, which was made at this time; many new buildings, particularly the present Pattiripooa.' The minister was stripped of his offices and imprisoned, was released after eight days and allowed to retire, then plotted the king's assassination; the plot failed, and in 1812 Pilimatalawe and his nephew were beheaded, with six petty chiefs hanged and impaled around their bodies. Davy also records that in 1814, after Molligoda's campaign into Sabaragamuwa against Ehelepola, prisoners were brought back to Kandy and 'forty-seven of whom were impaled'. Henry Marshall's Ceylon: A General Description (1846) gives the same 1812 execution and the same six impaled chiefs, and its appendices carry the British proclamation of 1815, which recites the killing of Ehelepola's wife and children — the children beheaded and their heads crushed in a mortar, the women weighted and drowned in a lake — as the ground for deposing the king.

What neither of those colonial-era narratives contains is the story this film was sent to test: that about a hundred chiefs who objected to the lake were impaled on its bund. It is not in Davy, who names the objection to the lake by name and would have had every reason to record the atrocity beside it, and it is not in Marshall's narrative or in the 1815 proclamation's bill of particulars, where a hundred impaled chiefs would have been the strongest item available. The claim circulates in modern Sri Lankan and travel writing in two versions that do not agree with each other. In one, a hundred headmen were impaled for refusing on principle to perform rajakariya on the new lake; in the other, a hundred of the king's advisers counselled him against building it and were impaled on the reservoir bund of the paddy field he was converting. The only citation offered for either, anywhere in this research, is in the second of two articles reproduced on a genealogy page — by Aryadasa Ratnasinghe, dated to the Daily News of 29 January 2005 — which gives the incident as occurring on Vesak poya day, 23 May 1814, and attributes it to 'a despatch by D'Oyly, the Resident of Kandy, the governor Sir Robert Brownrigg (vide Ceylon Literary Register, Vol. IV)'. Brownrigg did take the government on 11 March 1812, so a despatch to him in 1814 is chronologically possible, and the Ceylon Literary Register is a real periodical that printed material of exactly this kind. But the attribution could not be verified, D'Oyly was not Resident of Kandy in 1814, and 23 May 1814 was not a full-moon day: by calculation the full moons nearest it fell on 4 May and 2 June 1814.

The object itself is well described. The parapet that rings the water runs 633.82 m and is popularly called the Walakulu Bemma, the cloud wall, though it is argued that the correct name is Diyareli Bemma, the wave-swell wall; the triangular openings along it are reported to have been made for oil lamps at festival time. The lake covers a quarter of a square kilometre by the Sri Lankan sources and about nineteen hectares by others, with a circumference of about 3.25 km and a maximum depth of about 13 m, and it is reported to have been reduced in size since it was made. It is fed by two streams, the Heelpan Kandura out of the Hantana hills and the Rajapihilla, and sits within the Mahaweli catchment. It is a protected lake and fishing in it is prohibited. The island's later uses are variously reported — a royal retreat, a place where women of the harem were confined, a British ammunition store, and now a garden — and the stories of a bathing pavilion for the harem and a secret tunnel from the palace are recorded in the literature explicitly as legend. The Temple of the Tooth stands on the northern shore, and the kingdom was ceded to the British by the Kandyan Convention of 2 March 1815.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C005's whole teaching is that the aim in front of an act decides what kind of act it was, and this lake is the largest clean case of that on the island. The Margaya's list of everyday occasions for a grasping mind includes the preparing and the using of pleasing things — clothes, houses, carriages — and it includes, in so many words, looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking. Here is a public object whose recorded reason for existing is beauty, and whose daily use, two centuries later, is several thousand people walking round it and standing at the wall to look at the water. That is the item from the list, at civic scale, in the present tense.

Then the exemptions, which are the reason this location earns the concept instead of illustrating it. The Margaya does exempt, and it exempts generously: where faith, loving-kindness, compassion or practical discernment of usefulness goes in front, no unwholesome mind arises for the act; food cooked to quiet hunger and keep life going is not unwholesome; clothes made and worn against cold, heat, insects and what onlookers find repellent are not unwholesome; and even a beautiful, valuable garment is not unwholesome when it is worn to escape being looked down on for a shabby one. Read against this lake, those exemptions do not reach it. The four aims named in the exempting column are faith, kindness, compassion and use, and beauty is none of them; the Margaya puts beauty as an aim on the other side of the line explicitly — clothes prepared or worn in the expectation of being beautiful, of taking others' minds, of appearing as a superior person — and it does the same for food made for the relish or for the body's comeliness, and for the beautiful animal caught on sight and kept in order to be looked at. The one ruling that lets a beautiful and costly thing through does so for a reason that is not beauty at all, and the digest itself records that ruling as surprising and in need of an expert check before any film leans on it. So the honest answer, and the film's, is that making a thing beautiful falls outside the exemptions and inside the list. This lake has no irrigation command; it is not a tank that feeds fields. Had the record given it a stated practical purpose, the exemption on practical discernment of usefulness would have been squarely in play, and it is worth saying that some modern accounts do assert supplementary water storage and defence — but nothing found here supports that from a contemporary source, and the film does not use a purpose it cannot show was there.

What the classification is not, is a verdict, and the same digest says so twice. Its limits refuse 'art and sport are sinful' — music, dance and games are on the list because of the enjoying mind, not because the arts are condemned — and refuse 'minimalism' and 'self-denial is virtue', since valuable clothes and wisely earned wealth are explicitly allowed. And the cost of this lake is simply not weighed on the ornament page. The Margaya deals with harm on a different page, where seven of the ten courses of unwholesome action are said to be carried out with greed-rooted minds and taking what is not given is among them. Two pages, two instruments, and the source never totals them into a judgement on a person. That is what lets the film state the purpose, state the compelled labour, and state the disputed atrocity once, without becoming a prosecution — which is the only way this subject can be filmed at all under the floor.

C021 supplies the parts, and the place hands each one over physically. The bund is the settling made visible: one line of made ground, and the sources say the factor that settles comes down firmly on a thing without sorting true from false or good from bad, and is very often firm and wrong. That claim, laid beside a first minister telling the king to his face that the works were vexatious and oppressive, does work no analogy could — the objection is on the record, and so is the firmness. The quantity of labour is the sources' account of effort: mental rather than muscular, no colour of its own, running downhill like a boat on a current in a mind already leaning one way and needing to be carried uphill to go the other. Fifteen to thirty days a year, by tenure, moved a valley of paddy into a lake, and the sources decline to admire it. The island is the object that is arrived at and never reached, which is the pair of factors the sources picture as a bell's stroke and the ring after it, and as one hand gripping a vessel while the other polishes — arriving on something and staying with it, held simultaneous and not sequential, which is exactly how a lap of a ring path works. And the wish to do is the film's last word, because it is the group's: the sources insist it is not greed, that it lacks the stickiness, that in a grasping mind it goes along with the grasping and in a mind set the other way it works against it, and that trained it becomes a base of success and carries a person as far as a person can go. A king wanted a beautiful thing and it exists. The sources will not let that stand as either an indictment or an inspiration, and a lake is the right place to be told so, because the lake is neither.
what_is_certain: The lake is artificial. The site was a stretch of paddy fields known as Tigolwela, and a pond called Kiri-muhuda, the sea of milk, stood in the middle of it; the lake built over it took that name.
It was made by Sri Wickrama Rajasinha, who reigned from 1798 and was the last king of the country. The kingdom was ceded to the British under the Kandyan Convention of 2 March 1815.

The method was a dam across the low end of the valley, from the Paththirippuwa end of the palace precinct across to the Poya-maluwa, with a roadway along its top that allowed the king to cross to the Malwatte Vihare; earth was removed from both ends and an island was left in the middle, the Diyathilaka Mandapaya. Sri Lankan heritage sources name Deveda Moolacharya as the architect.

Rajakariya, the compulsory service owed to the crown, supplied the labour. John Davy, in the island from 1816 and publishing in 1821, describes the obligation as it stood: people 'were liable to be called on to labour at certain public works, as in making roads, levelling hills, and excavating tanks; and, according to the extent of their land-tenures, they might be employed annually in such services, from fifteen to thirty days.' Rajakariya was abolished in 1832 on the recommendation of the Colebrooke–Cameron Commission.

The objection to the works is recorded by Davy within a few years of them. Of the king's first minister Pilimatalawe: 'the minister expressed his disapprobation of the public works which the king was then engaged in, on the ground that they were vexatious to the people and oppressive. The works in question were several new roads; the lake of Kandy, which was made at this time; many new buildings, particularly the present Pattiripooa.'

Davy records that Pilimatalawe was stripped of his offices and imprisoned, released after eight days, subsequently plotted against the king, and in 1812 was beheaded together with his nephew, with six petty chiefs hanged and impaled around their bodies. Henry Marshall's Ceylon: A General Description (1846) gives the same episode, the same year and the same six impaled chiefs, adding that the bodies were tied to a post and exposed near a public road.
Davy records a separate impalement in 1814: after Molligoda's campaign into Sabaragamuwa against Ehelepola, prisoners were brought back to Kandy and 'forty-seven of whom were impaled'.

Marshall's appendices carry the British proclamation of 1815 deposing the king, which recites the killing of Ehelepola's wife and children — four infant children butchered and their heads bruised in a mortar by the mother's hands, then the woman and three other females bound, weighted with stones and drowned in a lake — as the grounds for deposition. This is a British state document making a case, and the film records it as such if it records it at all.
The parapet wall that rings the water measures 633.82 m and carries small triangular openings reported to have been intended for oil lamps at festival time.
The lake is fed by two streams, the Heelpan Kandura, rising in the Hantana hills, and the Rajapihilla, and lies within the Mahaweli catchment. It is a protected lake and fishing is prohibited.
The Temple of the Tooth stands on the northern shore of this lake, within the Sacred City of Kandy.
what_is_disputed: The central claim this record was sent to test, and it does not stand where it was placed: that about a hundred chiefs who objected to the lake were impaled on its bund. No contemporary or colonial-era narrative source found in this research carries it. It is absent from Davy (1821), who names the objection to the lake specifically and records other impalements with exact numbers, and absent from Marshall (1846) and from the 1815 British proclamation's bill of particulars, where it would have been the strongest available item. The claim circulates in modern Sri Lankan and travel writing in two versions that contradict each other on the reason: a hundred headmen impaled for refusing on principle to perform rajakariya on the new lake, or a hundred advisers impaled on the reservoir bund for counselling the king against building it. The number is constant at a hundred across the modern chain, which is itself a sign of a single origin rather than of independent attestation.

The one citation offered anywhere for the impalement, and why it could not be relied on. An article attributed to Aryadasa Ratnasinghe, dated to the Daily News of 29 January 2005 and reproduced on a genealogy page, dates the incident to Vesak poya day, 23 May 1814, and cites 'a despatch by D'Oyly, the Resident of Kandy, the governor Sir Robert Brownrigg (vide Ceylon Literary Register, Vol. IV)'. Brownrigg took the government on 11 March 1812, so a despatch to him in 1814 is chronologically possible, and the Ceylon Literary Register is a genuine periodical that printed material of this kind, so the citation is not impossible. But it could not be verified; D'Oyly was not Resident of Kandy in 1814, an office that followed the 1815 cession, which makes the descriptor anachronistic; and 23 May 1814 was not a full-moon day. By calculation the full moons nearest it fell on 4 May and 2 June 1814. That calculation is this research's own and should be checked.

Whether the lake as built was 1807 or 1810–1812. 1807 is the figure in nearly all travel and reference writing; 1810–1812 is attributed to D'Oyly and is followed by the Sri Lankan heritage literature. Neither was checked against a primary text here and they are not averaged.

The stated purpose, as evidence. That the lake was made to increase the beauty of the royal palace complex and the temples around it is unanimous in the modern literature and is consistent with the works themselves — a parapet with lamp niches, an island pavilion, and no irrigation command. But no contemporary statement of purpose, in the king's words or in a chronicle, was located in this research. The purpose is therefore well attested in the modern record and not quoted from a contemporary one.

Whether the lake also had practical purposes. Some modern accounts assert supplementary water storage and defence alongside the ornamental purpose. Nothing found here supports that from a contemporary source, and the film does not rely on it — which matters doctrinally, because a practical purpose would engage the source's exemption on practical discernment of usefulness.

The wall's proper name. It is popularly called the Walakulu Bemma, the cloud wall, and it is argued that the correct term is Diyareli Bemma, the wave-swell wall. Both are in use and the film does not settle it.

The lake's measurements. The Sri Lankan sources give a surface area of 0.25 square kilometres; other accounts give about nineteen hectares. Circumference is given as about 3.25 km and maximum depth as about 13 m. The lake is also reported to have been reduced in size since construction, without a figure. These are not reconciled.

The island's use, then and since. Recorded variously as a royal retreat or summer house, as a place where women of the king's household were confined, as a British ammunition store, and as a garden. The literature records the stories of a bathing pavilion for the harem and a secret tunnel from the palace explicitly as legend, and the film treats them as legend.

Above all, the reign itself is contested historiography and this film does not adjudicate it. Gananath Obeyesekere's The Doomed King: A Requiem for Sri Vikrama Rajasinha (2017) is the major scholarly re-examination of this king and argues against the received picture of his cruelty; it could not be read in this research because the copies located are lending-restricted, and it is named here as required reading before the film is made. The colonial-era sources this record does quote — Davy, Marshall, and a British proclamation issued to justify a deposition — are interested parties writing after or during a conquest. They are recorded as layers and are never treated as a verdict on the king, and the end of the kingdom in 1815 is not offered here as a consequence of anything.

what_to_film: The pre-sunrise half hour from the parapet: mist on black water, the far shore gone, the carved top of the wall the only hard edge in frame. This is the first beat and the film's own opening frame, and it has to be matched again at the end.
The wall along its length, long lens, low, so six hundred metres of the same carved swell stack into one rhythm; then the small triangular openings through it, close and empty.

The bund: the straight line of made ground closing the low end of the valley, filmed from both ends and from across the water, with the road and its early traffic on top and the town dropping away behind it.
The island from three separated points on the circuit, framed identically each time so it is visibly no nearer. No boat, no approach, no drone.
One held shot of the temple roofline at distance across the water, and nothing else of it. Not entered, not approached, no worship, no interior.
The upper end where the two streams come in off the hills: shallow clear water arriving into standing water; cormorants and egrets working the margin and roosting in the bank trees.
The mid-morning crowd along the parapet, filmed long from across the lake as a moving rhythm against stone. Nobody held, nobody followed, no face the subject of a frame.
The closing frame: the same stretch of parapet as the opening, mist gone, water bright, the lap complete. The payoff is the match, not a reveal.
suggested_location.access: The lake is a public place with no gate: a continuous footway of roughly three kilometres runs the whole perimeter, with roads alongside most of it and the bund road carrying traffic. Ground filming needs no site permission in principle, but the water lies inside the Sacred City of Kandy, immediately south of the Temple of the Tooth, with police and temple security present, so a filming permit and local liaison should be assumed and arranged in advance; the film's undertaking is that no arrangement is made which involves filming inside the temple precinct. Aerial work is treated as prohibited: this is dense city centre beside a principal place of worship in a World Heritage property, and the film is designed with no drone shot in it. If a high wide view is wanted at all it comes from a public viewpoint on the hill above the city on a long lens, at a time of day that does not need the lake to be empty. The island is not landed on.
suggested_location.best_time: The pre-sunrise half hour, for the mist and for an empty parapet, in the second monsoon months when mist forms most reliably and the water is highest; overcast and just-after-rain light for the stone, which sun flattens. The crowd beat needs full mid-morning light. The driest months give the worst mist and the lowest water and should be avoided. The film wants several consecutive mornings, because the opening and closing frames have to match and the mist cannot be ordered.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, carried out on 26 September 2026, and none of it checked on the ground. The coordinates are approximate to the middle of the water near the island rather than to any structure; the English Wikipedia article carries a rounded point (7.3, 80.6333) which is too coarse to use. Two of the sources were read in full rather than through secondary quotation, and they are the reason this record's findings differ from the brief it was given: John Davy's An Account of the Interior of Ceylon (1821) and Henry Marshall's Ceylon: A General Description (1846) were both downloaded as Internet Archive OCR text and searched line by line for the lake, for impalement and for the labour obligation. Every passage quoted from them in this record was read in its surrounding context; the OCR is poor in places, so the quoted wording should be checked against a printed edition before it is used in narration, and Marshall's text in particular is badly scanned. The 1810–1812 dating attributed to D'Oyly reaches this record through the Wikipedia history section and the Sri Lankan heritage literature, not from D'Oyly's own diary, which was not consulted; the diary was published by the Royal Asiatic Society (Ceylon Branch) in 1917 and reprinted in 1995 and should be read before the film is made. The impalement claim was pursued as far as it goes and the trail is recorded in full in what_is_disputed: the only citation offered anywhere is a 2005 newspaper column citing the Ceylon Literary Register, Vol. IV, which was not located or read, and no pre-modern or colonial-era narrative source containing the claim was found. The statement that 23 May 1814 was not a full-moon day is this research's own astronomical calculation and nothing else; it is offered as a reason for caution rather than as a finding, and it should be checked. Gananath Obeyesekere's The Doomed King (2017) is the scholarly work that most directly bears on everything in this record and it could not be read: the Internet Archive copy is lending-restricted, and a PDF found elsewhere would not yield text. It is flagged in what_is_disputed and in unknowns as required reading. The lake's measurements, the two feeder streams, the wall's length and the name dispute, the island's names and reported uses, the protected status and the fishing prohibition come from the Sri Lankan heritage and water-resource pages listed and were cross-read where two sources covered the same figure; where they disagree the disagreement is recorded and not averaged. One further fact was found and deliberately left out of the film: the city is reported to discharge very large volumes of wastewater daily into this catchment, and the lake's water quality is a live local issue. It is real and it is somebody else's film; using it here would turn a record about aims into an environmental indictment, which neither digest supports. Five Wikimedia Commons files were confirmed through action=query&titles= with a descriptive user agent before their URLs were written; sizes, uploaders, licences and the uploader's own descriptions were read, and the captions say what each image actually shows, including that the temple precinct appears at distance in one of them. Access, filming permits, police and temple liaison, drone rules and whether the pre-dawn footway is safe and workable for a crew are all unverified.

unknowns: No permission, permit, liaison or local contact has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
Whether mist forms reliably enough on the water at first light, in which months, and for how long, has not been checked against anything but reported description.
Whether the perimeter footway is workable for a crew before sunrise, and what the police and temple security actually require of a camera on that walk, is unknown.
Whether the pre-dawn parapet can be filmed empty at all, given how heavily used the circuit is.
The 1807 and 1810–1812 datings are both unchecked against a primary text, and D'Oyly's own diary has not been read.
The Ceylon Literary Register, Vol. IV, was not located, so the single citation ever offered for the impalement claim remains unexamined rather than disproved.
Obeyesekere's The Doomed King (2017) has not been read and bears directly on every historical claim in this record.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified. The two colonial-era narratives quoted were read in full text, but from OCR rather than print, and they are interested parties writing during or after a conquest. No scene or shot is decided here.
